title: White-box testing: covering every path
summary: Design test cases from the code itself: ifs, loops, exceptions and their combinations, and when white-box beats black-box.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: Black-box design guesses behaviour from the specification; white-box design reads the code and tests every path through it. A path is roughly one way of getting from the start of a method to its end, and every path becomes a test case. Conditionals create paths: each if splits one path into two, and further constructs split them again. The number of paths often differs from the number of black-box categories, which is exactly why both techniques exist.

sections.heading: Ifs and if-else
paras: An if has two paths: enter the branch or skip it. The myAbs method (negate n when n < 0, then return) needs one case with a negative input taking the branch and one with a non-negative input skipping it. An if-else also has two paths: the if side or the else side. The printMax method needs one case entering the if (x > y, prints x) and one entering the else (prints y).

sections.heading: Loops count as two
paras: Loops look infinite but contribute exactly two paths: the loop body runs, or it does not. It makes no difference whether the body runs twice or a million times; it is the same path. The readPositive method (keep asking while input is not positive) therefore needs an entering case with scripted input like -5\n10 producing a Not positive message, and a skipping case with input 5 producing no message. Python has no do-while; Java's version adds a no-repeat versus some-repeat pair of the same shape.

sections.heading: Exceptions and combinations
paras: Each try-catch (try-except in Python) contributes one path for success plus one per catch/except clause. The convertF2C method needs a success case (numeric input prints the converted temperature) and one case per handled exception type (non-numeric input prints the error). Constructs combine by splitting: a nested if inside an if turns two paths into three, as zeroOrLargest shows (outer else prints 0; inner if prints x; inner else prints y). Notice black-box would list four sign combinations for the same method while white-box finds three paths: the techniques genuinely disagree, and the exam loves asking why.

sections.heading: Choosing between black and white
paras: Design black-box tests before the code exists and keep them stable while algorithms change, since they only depend on the specification. Choose white-box when you need to see the decisions the code actually makes, or when black-box guessing misses behaviours hidden in the implementation. The price of white-box precision is maintenance: changing the production code usually means changing its tests, though the result is tests that track what the code really does.

callout.text: For any code snippet, enumerate constructs (if, else-if, loop, try-catch), count paths (if=2, loop=2, each catch=+1, a nested if splits one existing path into two (+1: two paths become three)), then give one row per path with inputs and expected output. State explicitly when the white-box count differs from the black-box category count.

recall.q: How many paths do if, loop and try-catch contribute?
recall.a: An if or if-else contributes two paths; a loop contributes two (enter or skip, regardless of iteration count); a try block contributes one success path plus one per catch/except clause.

recall.q: Why does zeroOrLargest have 3 white-box paths but 4 black-box categories?
recall.a: Black-box combines the signs of x and y into four categories; the code only decides y > 0 first, then x > y inside, giving three reachable paths (outer else, inner if, inner else). One sign combination is unreachable as a distinct path.

recall.q: When should you prefer white-box over black-box?
recall.a: When you need to cover decisions hidden in the code that the specification does not reveal. Prefer black-box when the code does not exist yet or changes often, since those tests survive reimplementation.

activities.instructions: Drag each word into its blank.
text: An if has ___ paths; a loop has ___ paths; each catch adds ___ path.
activities.explanation: if = enter or skip; loop = enter or skip regardless of iterations; try = success plus one per catch clause.
hints: Loops are simpler than they look.

activities.prompt: A loop that runs a million times is a different path from one that runs twice.
activities.confirm: Entering the loop is one path no matter how many iterations follow.
activities.explanation: White-box counts entering versus skipping the body; iteration count does not create new paths.
